The concurring Justices found the distinction between the interests 
asserted by the plaintiffs here and the interests recognized as conferring 
standing in prior cases as extremely “nice” ones. The distinctions were entirely 
too nice for Justices Stevens and Breyer. The former could not conceive of how 
voters could have standing to pursue the question of the apportionment of their 
state legislature, as individu^ voters surely do under Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 
186 (1962), and yet hold that there was no particularized injury to 
representatives denied the opportunity to vote on the bills that actually went 
into effect after the president’s exercise of his line-item veto. Justice Breyer 
simply could find no difference between this case and Coleman v. Miller. 
Because he, like the majority, would not overrule Coleman, he would have 
found standing in these plaintiffs.
A number of subsequent cases have rehed on the Raines analysis. In 
Virginia House of Delegates v. Bethune-Hill, 139 S. Ct. 1945 (2019), the 
Supreme Court rejected an attempt by one house of a bicameral state 
legislature to assert standing on behalf of the entire legislature. The Vhg^a 
House of Delegates was attempting to appeal an injunction requiring Virginia 
to develop a new redistricting plan following a gerrymandering challenge. The 
Court found that “Dl^st as individual members lack standing to assert the 
institutional interests of a legislature, a single House of a bicameral legislature 
lacks capacity to assert interests belonging to the legislature as a whole. Id. 
at 1953. The court also found that “Changes to [the Virginia House’s] 
membership brought about by the voting public [as a result of redistricting]... 
Inflict no cognizable injury” on the House.
In U.S. House of Representatives v. Mnuchin, 976 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2020) 
declared moot by Yellen v. United States House of Representatives, 142 S. Ct. 
332 (2021), the D.C. Circuit found that a house of a bicameral legislature can 
obtain fitanding if injury is specific to the house. Here, the issue was a violation 
of the appropriations clause, and the court found that the Appropriations 
Clause requires two keys to unlock the Treasury, and the House holds one of 
those keys.” Id. at 13.
In Blumenthal v. Trump, 949 F.3d 14 (D.C. Circuit 2020), the D.C. Circuit 
considered a suit by 215 members of Congress against President Trump based 
on his alleged violations of the Emoluments Clause. The court denied standing, 
finding that “[a]fter Raines and Bethune-Hill, only an institution can assert m 
institutional injury provided the injury is not ‘wholly abstract and wide y 
dispersed.’ ” Id. at 19.
